## El link que enviaste

`https://network.developer.nokia.com/learn/24_11/index/` pide **login Nokia (SSO)**. Sin credenciales no entra: solo veo la pantalla de autenticación.

Si más adelante tenés PDFs, capturas de la GUI, o un export del portal, los puedo usar como referencia.

## Lo que sí pude leer (público)

La colección oficial de **NSP Release 24.11** en `documentation.nokia.com/nsp/24-11/` (Issue 13, mayo 2026). Incluye, entre otros:

| Guía | Para qué sirve |
|---|---|
| **Classic Management (NFM-P User Guide)** | GUI clásica para redes IP/MPLS: operaciones, dispositivos, políticas, servicios |
| Device Management Guide | Inventario y gestión de NEs (NSP vs NFM-P clásico) |

| XML API Developer Guide | API OSS (XML/SOAP, JMS) |

| Release Description 24.11 | Features de la release |

## Qué es NFM-P 24.11 (resumen)

**NFM-P** (Network Functions Manager – Packet, evolución del 5620 SAM) es el gestor clásico de Nokia para redes **IP/MPLS**. En 24.11 vive como componente de **NSP**.

La GUI original es un **cliente Java** (no web), con:

- Barra de menú (`File`, `Manage`, `Application`, `Tools`…)
- Árbol de navegación (Equipment / Routing / Services)
- Mapas de topología (físico, IGP, OSPF, ISIS, **MPLS**, túneles, LSP, servicios)
- Forms de lista y de configuración (pestañas, multi-edit, clipboard)
- Alarmas, inventario, discovery, políticas, servicios (VPLS, VPRN, Epipe, IES…)
- MPLS: interfaces, LSPs RSVP/LDP/SR, service tunnels, MPLS-TP
- Equipment Manager, Task Manager, búsquedas avanzadas, span of control

En NSP 24.11 hay además una **GUI web** (Network Map and Health, Device Management, Service Management, Path Control). Vos pediste replicar **NFM-P**, o sea la experiencia clásica.

## Limitación importante

Puedo reconstruir **estructura, flujos y look** a partir de la doc pública. No tengo:

- Acceso al portal de desarrolladores (APIs internas, labs, ejemplos autenticados)
- Capturas reales de tu NFM-P
- El look exacto píxel a píxel del cliente Java 24.11

Cuando quieras, decime cómo seguimos: alcance (solo GUI demo, o con datos/API), módulos (topología, MPLS, alarmas, servicios, inventario), y si preferís look Java clásico o look NSP web.

Son 3 cosas. Preferí **PDF** o **capturas**. El HTML a veces no trae las figuras.

| # | Documento | Qué extraer | Por qué |

| 2 | El mismo User Guide | Capítulo **31 MPLS**, **32 MPLS-TP**, **33 Service tunnels** (overview + workflows + figuras de forms) | Es el dominio que vos querés gestionar |
| 3 | **Capturas de tu NFM-P real** (si tenés lab o cliente) | Ver lista abajo | Vale más que cualquier PDF: color, iconos, menús reales de 24.11 |

### Capturas que más me sirven (si podés)

Desde un cliente NFM-P 24.11, así como lo ves vos:

1. Ventana principal completa (menú + toolbar + árbol + mapa/forms + alarmas)
2. Menú `File / View / Manage / Application / Tools / Administration / Help` desplegado (o todos)
3. Árbol de navegación: vistas Equipment y Routing
4. Mapa de topología física (Equipment)
5. Mapa MPLS / Service Tunnel Topology
6. Un **list form** (ej. Manage → Equipment, o Manage → MPLS → Dynamic LSPs)
7. Un **configuration form** con pestañas (ej. properties de un 7750, o de un LSP)
8. Ventana de **alarmas** (Faults)
9. Equipment Manager / inventario de un NE (shelf → card → port)
10. Form “Create Dynamic LSP” o “Create Service Tunnel (SDP)”

Si no tenés GUI a mano, con el PDF del User Guide (caps 1–4 + 31–33) alcanza para el esqueleto.

## Lote 2 — después, cuando definamos módulos

No los busques todavía. Los pido cuando toque cada módulo:

| Documento | Cuándo |
|---|---|
| **CPAM User Guide 24.11** — caps Topology + MPLS topology | Mapas IGP/OSPF/ISIS/MPLS con highlight de LSPs |
| **XML API Developer Guide 24.11** (`3HE-20022`) — overview + inventory + MPLS + services | Modelo de objetos (`equipment`, `mpls`, `service`, `fm`) |

| **Statistics Management Guide** | Si hacemos stats/gráficos |
| **NSP User Guide 24.11** (la GUI **web** de NSP, no la Java) | Solo si querés mix NSP web + NFM-P clásico |

## Lo que no hace falta

Installation, Planning, Security Hardening, CLM, Wavence, Analytics Report Catalog, System Administrator (salvo users/roles si más adelante hay login).

## Cómo pasármelo

Lo que mejor funciona acá:

- **PDF** del User Guide (aunque sea solo caps 1–4 y 31–33)
- **PNG/JPG** de las capturas
- Si el PDF es enorme, recortes de esas secciones

No hace falta zip de toda la documentación Nokia.

1→# Getting Started

Grok Build is a terminal-based AI coding assistant from SpaceXAI. It runs as a TUI (Terminal User Interface) that understands your codebase, executes shell commands, edits files, searches the web, and manages tasks.

You can use it interactively as a full-screen TUI, run it headlessly for scripting and CI/CD, or integrate it into editors via the Agent Client Protocol (ACP).

---

## Installation
10→
Install the latest stable release (macOS, Linux, or Windows via Git Bash):

```bash
curl -fsSL https://x.ai/cli/install.sh | bash
```

Install a specific version:

```bash
20→curl -fsSL https://x.ai/cli/install.sh | bash -s 0.1.42
```

On **Windows (PowerShell)**, use the native PowerShell installer:

```powershell
irm https://x.ai/cli/install.ps1 | iex
```

Install a specific version:
30→
```powershell
$env:GROK_VERSION="0.1.42"; irm https://x.ai/cli/install.ps1 | iex
```

The PowerShell installer automatically adds `%USERPROFILE%\.grok\bin` to your User PATH. Alternatively, install via [Git for Windows](https://gitforwindows.org/) (Git Bash) or MSYS2 using the bash script above. WSL users get the Linux binary automatically.

Verify the installation:

```bash
40→grok --version
```

Update to the latest version at any time:

```bash
grok update
```

To fetch a repository through Grove (NFS on macOS, FUSE on Linux) after
50→`[clone] enabled = true` in Grove config:

```bash
grok clone <url> [dir]
```

The default is a depth-1 checkout of the selected branch. Pass `--full-history`
for a complete clone. See [grok clone](27-grok-clone.md).

---
60→
## First Launch

Start Grok by running:

```bash
grok
```

On first launch, Grok opens your browser to authenticate with grok.com. After you sign in, Grok stores your credentials in `~/.grok/auth.json`, where they persist across sessions. Grok refreshes your credentials automatically and prompts you to sign in again when they can no longer be renewed.
70→
If you prefer API key authentication (e.g., for CI/CD or environments without a browser), set the `XAI_API_KEY` environment variable instead:

```bash
export XAI_API_KEY="xai-..."
grok
```

See [Authentication](02-authentication.md) for the full set of auth options including OIDC, external auth providers, and device code flow.

80→---

1→# Slash Commands

Type `/` in the prompt to open the command menu. It fuzzy-matches as you type, and picking a command runs it immediately.

Commands come from two places: **shell builtins**, handled by the agent backend (xai-grok-shell), and **pager builtins**, handled by the pager frontend (xai-grok-pager). Both show up in the same menu, and any enabled skill with `user-invocable: true` appears there too. If a skill reuses a built-in name such as `login`, the built-in keeps `/login` and the skill stays available as `/plugin-name:login` — the menu badges both so the collision is visible.

Every command below lists its aliases where it has them. A few commands only appear when a feature or session state enables them; those cases are called out inline. The menu is also filtered by render mode — see [`/minimal` and `/fullscreen`](#minimal-and-fullscreen).

---
10→
## Session Management

### `/new`

Start a fresh session and clear the current conversation. Alias: `/clear`.

### `/resume`

Open the session picker to reload a previous session from disk.
20→
### `/dashboard`

Open the [Agent Dashboard](23-dashboard.md): live roster of top-level sessions in this pager (peek, reply, dispatch, pin, rename, stop, attach). Aliases: `/agents-dashboard`, `/sessions`.

Not `/config-agents` (alias `/agents`), which manages agent *definitions* and personas. Hidden in minimal mode; disable with `GROK_AGENT_DASHBOARD=0` or `[dashboard].enabled = false`.

### `/compact [context]`

Compress conversation history to reclaim context-window space. Pass a note to tell Grok what to keep:
30→
```
/compact
/compact keep the auth implementation details
```

Grok also auto-compacts once the context window hits 85% (tune it with `[session] auto_compact_threshold_percent`).

### `/context`

40→Show how the context window is being used: a category breakdown (system prompt, messages, reasoning and overhead, free space) plus informational rows for tool definitions, the skills listing, and MCP server announcements with their estimated token cost.

### `/session-info`

Show session details — auth method, model, turn count, and context usage. Aliases: `/status`, `/info`. Click a value or drag to select and copy; `c` copies the session ID and `y` copies the whole block.

### `/fork`

Branch the current session into a new agent, keeping history up to this point.

50→### `/rewind` (alias: `/undo`)

Roll the conversation back to an earlier turn and discard everything after it. `/undo` is the same command.

### `/copy`

Copy the most recent response's source markdown to the clipboard. Pass a number to copy the Nth-latest response instead, or a file path to write the text to a file rather than the clipboard (handy over SSH, where the local clipboard is often unreachable).

```
/copy
60→/copy 2
/copy out.txt
/copy 2 ~/exports/last-reply.md
```

Every copy is also written to a backup file — `~/.grok/last-copy.txt` by default, or `GROK_COPY_FILE` if set. Confirmed copies toast briefly (e.g. `Copied!`). Unverified OSC 52 deliveries and clipboard-unreachable fallbacks name the backup path so you can recover the text.

### `/export`

Export the conversation to a file or the clipboard.
70→
### `/quit`

Quit the application. Alias: `/exit`.

### `/home`

Leave the current session and return to the welcome screen. Alias: `/welcome`.

### `/delete`
80→

1→# Keyboard Shortcuts

Reference for key bindings in the Grok Build TUI. Bindings are built in and cannot currently be remapped.

---

## Input Modes

Grok has two input modes that control how you navigate the scrollback:
10→
- **Simple mode** (default): Arrow keys for navigation, `Shift+Arrow` for turn navigation, `Space` to focus the prompt, and any letter key auto-focuses the prompt.
- **Vim mode** (opt-in): `j`/`k` for navigation, `H`/`L` for turn navigation, `J`/`K` for response navigation, `h`/`l` for fold, `e`/`E` for expand/collapse, and `i`/`Tab`/`Space` to focus the prompt.

Simple mode is active by default. To switch to Vim mode, set `vim_mode = true` under `[ui]` in `~/.grok/config.toml`, or toggle it at runtime with `/vim-mode`. See [Configuration](05-configuration.md) for details.

The tables below document bindings for both modes. The "Key" column shows the Vim-mode binding, and the "Alt Key" column shows the equivalent in simple mode (arrow keys, etc.).

> **Vim-mode required**: Single-letter and `Shift+letter` bindings in the
> **Scrollback** context (`j/k`, `h/l`, `g/G`, `L/H`, `y/Y`, `o/O`, `r`,
20→> `x`, `e/E`, and the `i` insert-mode alt) require `[ui].vim_mode = true`
> in `~/.grok/config.toml` (or `/vim-mode` to toggle). Arrow keys, `Tab`,
> `Esc`, `Space`, `PageUp/Down`, and every `Ctrl+letter` shortcut work in
> both modes.

---

## Navigation (Scrollback Focused)

Move through conversation entries in the scrollback pane.
30→
| Key | Alt Key | Action |
|-----|---------|--------|
| `j` | `Down` | Select next entry |
| `k` | `Up` | Select previous entry |
| `⇧L` | `Shift+Right` | Jump to next turn (user prompt) |
| `⇧H` | `Shift+Left` | Jump to previous turn (user prompt) |
| `⇧J` | | Jump to next assistant response |
| `⇧K` | | Jump to previous assistant response |
| `g` | | Go to top of scrollback |
40→| `⇧G` | | Go to bottom of scrollback |
| `Ctrl+K` | | Scroll up one line (without changing selection) |
| `Ctrl+J` | | Scroll down one line (without changing selection) |
| `PageUp` | | Scroll up one page (selection moves to the top of the viewport) |
| `PageDown` | | Scroll down one page (selection moves to the bottom of the viewport) |
| `Ctrl+U` | | Scroll up half page |
| `Ctrl+D` (`Shift+D` in VSCode) | | Scroll down half page |

`PageUp` and `PageDown` also scroll the conversation while the ordinary prompt
is focused, without moving focus or changing the draft. An active prompt
50→history, `@` file search, slash menu, or completion dropdown keeps the keys for
its own navigation.

---

## View (Scrollback Focused)

Control how entries are displayed in the scrollback.

| Key | Alt Key | Action |
60→|-----|---------|--------|

1→# Status Line

An optional row at the bottom of the pager — above the shortcuts bar in the full screen, under the prompt's info row in minimal mode — and disabled by default. It shows live session context, such as the model, context-window usage, cost, directory, and git worktree, or the output of any script you configure. Opt in with `[ui.status_line]` in `~/.grok/config.toml`.

## Set up

### Built-in

```toml
10→[ui.status_line]
type = "builtin"
items = ["cwd", "model", "context"]   # default when omitted
```

This renders, for example, `grok-shell-status-line │ Grok 4.5 │ 12% ctx`. Items appear in the order you list them, and long ones are elided with `…`: the directory and session name at 40 columns, the model at 30.

| Item | Shows |
| --- | --- |
| `cwd` | Current directory (basename) |
20→| `model` | Model display name |
| `context` | Context-window percent, amber at the auto-compaction threshold or at 80% when the agent reports none |
| `cost` | Session cost, hidden below $0.005 so it never shows a misleading `$0.00` |
| `turn-timer` | Elapsed time of the running turn, from one second in |
| `session-name` | Session name, when set |

### Command

Point `command` at a script. Grok pipes [JSON](#available-data) to it on stdin and shows its stdout. A `~/` prefix expands to your home directory.

30→```toml
[ui.status_line]
type = "command"
command = "~/.grok/statusline.sh"
```

Field names and nesting follow the common status line convention, so a ported script usually needs a small edit rather than a rewrite. Anything the table below does not list is not sent.

### Disabled

40→`type = "disabled"`, the default, shows nothing; `off`, `none`, and `hidden` are accepted as spellings of `disabled`.

### Options

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `type` | string | `disabled` | `builtin`, `command`, or `disabled`. |
| `items` | array | `["cwd", "model", "context"]` | Built-in segments, in order. |
| `command` | string | none | Script for `type = "command"`. |
| `padding` | integer | `0` | Horizontal spacing, in characters per side, capped at 16. A padding wide enough to leave no columns reserves the row but paints nothing in it. |
50→| `refresh_interval` | integer | unset | `command` rows only, in seconds, 1 to 86,400. Re-runs the script this often even when nothing changed, so an idle session can still surface a change — an incident page, a CI status. Unset keeps the row event-driven. The run it schedules carries `"trigger": "refresh_interval"`, and its failures keep the last output rather than painting an error (see [Refresh runs](#refresh-runs)). A script that calls a network should prefer a longer interval and read a cache on `state` runs. |

## How it works

- **Refresh.** The row updates when the session state changes (session start, turn end, a model or effort switch, a HEAD move, a compaction, a client attaching) and continuously while a turn runs, not on a timer. An idle session does not re-run your script, so a clock in it will not tick on its own — unless you set `refresh_interval`, which adds a timer on top of all of the above. These updates are debounced at a fixed 300 ms, so a busy turn cannot run your script every frame; a change that must show at once (a resize, a new snapshot, switching agents) waits only 100 ms. A run already going is never cancelled: the next change waits for it to finish. Grok reads `[ui.status_line]` at startup, so changes to it take effect at the next launch.
- **Output.** Each line you print becomes one line of the row, up to five, and each is cut at 1024 characters, counting the ANSI escapes themselves, so a heavily coloured row has less room for text. A short terminal takes fewer, dropping the surplus from the bottom. ANSI colors are honored; every other escape (cursor motion, line erase, carriage-return overwrite) is dropped. OSC 8 hyperlinks are honored for `http`, `https` and `mailto` targets, and any other target renders as plain text. Stdout past 64 KiB is truncated and the script is stopped. A script that succeeds and prints nothing takes the row away rather than falling back to the built-in segments, so a script that prints only sometimes moves the transcript by a line as it comes and goes.
- **Sizing.** Grok sets `COLUMNS` and `LINES` to the row your output fills, not to the window: the pane's padding and your `padding` are already deducted. `tput` reports these too, since it reads them when stdout is not a terminal. `LINES` is what the row currently fills rather than what it may grow to, so it reads `1` until you print more; the ceiling is five whatever it says. Before the row has painted once, and on a frame with no room for it, the size is the last one the row painted at, or 80x1 if it never has.
- **Shell.** `command` is a shell command line, so `jq -r '…'` and pipes work as written; a path is run directly when it names an executable, and through `sh -c` otherwise, which is what runs a script whose `#!` line is missing or wrong. Quote a path containing spaces as you would at a prompt. Each run is a fresh process, so an edit to the script file applies on the next run.
- **Background work does not survive.** Whatever a script leaves running is killed when the run ends, on every path: a clean exit, a timeout, or too much output. The run ends when your script exits, so anything a background job prints after that is lost.
- **Environment.** Scripts run in the session's working directory, then the repository root, then the pager's own, whichever is a local path first, with a 10 second timeout, after which the row shows `[status line: timed out]`. `COLUMNS` and `LINES` describe the row the script fills, not the window. No shell rc files run (`BASH_ENV` and `ENV` are cleared), and `GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0`. Pagers and editors are neutralized the same way the rest of Grok neutralizes them, so a `git` or `gh` call inside your script will not block waiting for one.
60→- **Input.** The JSON payload is written to stdin with a trailing newline, so `read -r line` and `input=$(cat)` both work.

## Refresh runs

Set `refresh_interval` on a `command` row and the script also re-runs on a timer, so an incident page or a CI status can reach the row while the session sits idle:

```toml
[ui.status_line]
type = "command"
command = "~/.grok/statusline.sh"
70→refresh_interval = 300   # seconds
```

- **The payload says why the script ran.** A run that answers the timer carries `"trigger": "refresh_interval"` — a state change landing while a timer fire is owed rides that run — and a run with no fire owed carries `"trigger": "state"`. Hit the network on `refresh_interval` and read a cache on `state`, or a busy turn — which re-runs the script continuously — becomes a request storm against whatever the script calls.
- **The payload is the last one Grok sent.** A timer run re-runs your script with the payload from the last state change, so its session numbers — cost, context, tokens — are as of that change, not of the fire. Only what your script fetches itself is fresh.
- **Refresh failures keep the last output.** Once your script has answered — printed a row, or deliberately nothing — a timer run that fails or times out leaves the row exactly as it was, whether that is the last output or a failure a state run had already painted, and writes the failure to `~/.grok/logs/unified.jsonl`, so a flaky endpoint does not paint an error over a quiet night. Three consecutive refresh failures mean the script itself is broken, and the error shows after all; a refresh failure before the script has answered anything — a fresh session, or right after switching agents — also paints at once, since there is nothing to keep. A run triggered by session state still reports its failure at once, as ever.
- **Missed fires coalesce.** While the row is hidden (a fullscreen subagent view, the welcome screen) or a run already holds the slot, the fire waits and the row is owed one run when it can have it — never a burst for the fires a suspend or a long turn skipped. The timer keeps its cadence whatever your script's runtime: a fire that comes due while a run is still going is carried to the next run rather than stacked behind it.
- **The timer belongs to the mode that runs a script.** `refresh_interval` under `builtin` schedules nothing and is reported through `grok inspect`; under `disabled` it is off with everything else.

430→1.4.1 Types of forms
431→The NFM-P displays forms in response to menu options or other on-screen selections. Forms
432→display lists or allow you to view and configure properties. Some forms display other information.
433→
434→The GUI displays the following form types:
435→• list forms
436→• configuration forms
437→• step forms
438→• property forms
439→• problems encountered forms
440→• other forms such as messages, warnings, or dialog boxes. These forms are also sometimes
441→referred to as windows.
442→
443→See Figure 1-1, “List form” (p. 83)and Figure 1-4, “Service configuration form with built-in tree”

447→features; see 1.13 “To manage the display of windows and forms” (p. 105). A form can be displayed
448→anywhere in the GUI. A newly opened form is displayed in the foreground. You can do the following:

458→menu on the main menu lists all open forms.

775→1.6.11 Modifying configuration forms with built-in navigation trees
776→When you modify a docked configuration form, it becomes locked. The lock icon appears in orange
777→until the changes are saved. An orange lock icon indicates unsaved changes on the form. You

779→but the icon is no longer orange.

781→If you attempt to close a modified configuration form that contains unsaved changes, a message
782→prompts you to specify whether to discard the changes or return to the display. If you attempt to
783→close a modified configuration form that has related forms with unsaved modifications, the message
784→lists the forms that have unsaved changes.
785→
786→For service configuration forms, if an object is added to the service configuration, the new object
787→appears in the built-in navigation tree and the configuration form is displayed with the orange lock
788→icon. The icon remains orange until the modifications are saved or discarded.

790→For NE property forms, if an object is added from the navigation tree, the change will be made
791→immediately. However, if a change, such as adding or removing an object, is made to an equipment
792→configuration form, the change will be reflected on the form immediately, but it will not be reflected
793→on the navigation tree until the OK, Apply, or Apply Tab button is clicked.

772→8.11 What is User Access Control?
773→
774→8.11.1 Overview
775→User Access Control (UAC) defines what commands a user can perform in an NSP system and
776→what objects those commands can be performed on. NSP UAC is defined through role definitions
777→that are assigned to user groups, and each user is associated with one user group.
778→
779→In an NSP deployment, UAC applies to a user when accessing NSP function. NSP users that
780→access NFM-P or WSNOC will have access determined by what is configured for that user group in
781→NFM-P or WSNOC applications. (eg. An NSP user accessing NFM-P will have access to the
782→NFM-P scope and span profiles that belong to the user’s NFM-P user group).
783→
784→NSP User Access Control is disabled by default, meaning that users can access any NSP function
785→that is not restricted by a specific user group requirement. Users that belong to the admin user
786→group can access all function, including admin-only functions. Users that do not belong to the admin
787→user group can access all non-admin applications. A user that does not belong to the admin user
788→group but has a system administrator role privilege will not be able to access admin-only functions.
789→
790→When NSP UAC is enabled, the role definitions belonging to an NSP user group determine the NSP
791→functions and commands a user can access, and which network objects the user can access.
792→
793→In CLM deployments, UAC applies to CLM users.
794→
795→When UAC is enabled, access is assigned at the NSP level and applies across the NSP GUI. Users
796→will see their specified NSP access permissions enforced when they login to NSP. The user access
797→configuration specified in NSP is enforced in place ofany pre-existing access control setup (from
798→NFM-P or WS-NOC). Local NSP user access to NSP resources is always controlled through NSP,
799→regardless of whether UAC is enabled or not.
800→
801→As a network evolves, an NSP administrator must create or modify user groups, roles, and resource
802→groups to provide the required user access to NSP functions. Be aware of functional crossdependencies.
803→
804→When UAC is enabled, it controls user access to NSP functions independently of the user
805→management systems in NFM-P or WS-NOC.
806→
807→UAC does not apply to WS-NOC or NFM-P GUI or OSS client sessions if pre-existing user access
808→control mechanisms are in use. If you maintain your NSP user accounts in an NFM-P user
809→database, all NFM-P functions related to user lifecycle management, such as password expiry time
810→or failed-login lockout, also affect NSP user access. Local NSP user accounts are configured for
811→UAC and lifecycle management entirely within the NSP.

850→8.11.2 Roles
851→A role object specifies which resources and NSP functions its associated user groups can access.
852→Network resource access is assigned to a role through resource groups, while functional access
853→and Analytics resource access are specified directly on a role object.
854→
855→NSP administrator role
856→
857→A predefined NSP administrator role, user group, and admin user account are automatically created
858→during NSP system installation and cannot be modified. The admin user has full access to all NSP
859→functions and resources, and can define the roles and resource groups that are assigned to user
860→groups. The admin user can create additional roles with the Administrator designation, which carries
861→the same unlimited functional and resource access.
862→
863→8.11.3 User groups
864→A user group associates a group of NSP users with one or more roles, thereby enabling user
865→access to functional areas and resources. Administrators create user groups and assign roles to
866→them, according to the type of network activities the user group is meant to perform. When a role is
867→assigned to a user group, all users within the group have the same access to resources and
868→functions, as specified on the role. A user group can be assigned multiple roles to allow broader
869→access rights for its users.
870→
871→Individual NSP users can be created by external authentication sources (NFM-P, LDAP, RADIUS,
872→TACACS) where users are assigned to corresponding user groups. In order for the members of a
873→user group to have access to NSP resources and functions, the user group name returned by the
874→authentication source must exactly match a corresponding user group name in NSP.
875→
876→Local NSP users and user groups can also be created in the NSP.
877→
878→Users requiring WS-NOC access require a user group assignment that maps to a predefined WS-
879→NOC role; for information, see To map external user groups to predefined WS-NOC roles in the
880→NSP Installation and Upgrade Guide .

12→The NFM-P navigation tree provides multiple views that list the equipment groups, NEs, routing

16→functions using the navigation tree window.

37→arrow keys move the selection up or down in the tree. The right and left arrow keys expand or

583→General examples of segments in Layer 2 service topologies include:

589→Just a few examples of the many possible service-specific segmentation configurations include
590→scenarios such as the following:
591→• H-VPLS (Inter-Metro with redundant spoke SDPs):
592→− One application of H-VPLS is the connection of two or more geographically-dispersed VPLS
593→domains belonging to the same customer. Two spoke SDP connections are used to connect
594→each VPLS between the two metros, either in a redundant PW spokes topology or under STP
595→protocol. The redundant spokes comprise one segment, while each VPLS will also comprise
596→one or more segments, depending on their specific configurations.
597→• VLL Switching:
598→− For a VLL service at a switching router, a terminating PE device has at least one VLL SAP,
599→while a switching PE device has a VLL instance which cross-connects two spoke bindings. All
600→VLL instances of such a service must have the same service ID, and if the VLL has one or
601→more switching sites, it must have at least two terminating sites. In this scenario, the primary
602→and redundant spoke SDPs on the same network endpoint are considered to be in the same
603→segment.
604→• PBB:
605→− In a PBB configuration, the B-VPLS is considered a service tunnel, from the I-VPLS or
606→I-Epipe perspective. Therefore, the sites connected via a B-VPLS (that is, having the same
607→ISID) are considered to be in one segment.
608→− I-Sites bound to the same PBB tunnel (B-VPLS) and having the same ISID exist in the same
609→segment.
610→− Epipe sites bound to same PBB tunnel (B-VPLS) exist in the same segment

¡Perfecto! Entiendo exactamente lo que quieres: un CLI interactivo en Python inspirado en Grok 4.6, con login, shell navegable y sin replicar la interfaz actual. Vamos a construir **NSP-Grok 24.11**, un sistema de gestión de red basado en los documentos 7750 SR que tienes.

### Estructura del proyecto
```

def _user(username: str, password: str, **kwargs) -> User:

def _ports(names: list[tuple[str, str, str, str, str]]) -> list[Port]:
    out: list[Port] = []
    for name, mode, speed, admin, oper in names:
        encap = "null" if mode == "network" else "dot1q"
        out.append(
            Port(
                name=name,
                mode=mode,
                encap=encap,
                admin=admin,  # type: ignore[arg-type]
                oper=oper,  # type: ignore[arg-type]
                speed=speed,
                description=f"{mode} {name}",
            )
        )
    return out

        equipped=card_type,
        admin="up",
        oper="degraded" if down else "up",

def seed_stats(nes: dict[str, NetworkElement], lsps: dict[str, Lsp]) -> list[StatSample]:
    now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
    samples: list[StatSample] = []
    for ne in nes.values():
        for card in ne.cards:
            for port in card.ports:
                if port.oper != "up":
                    continue
                base = 1_000_000 if "100G" in port.speed else 80_000 if "10G" in port.speed else 8_000
                fdn = f"ne:{ne.name}:port:{port.name}"
                samples.append(StatSample(fdn, "ifInOctets", base * 940, "bytes", now))
                samples.append(StatSample(fdn, "ifOutOctets", base * 710, "bytes", now))
                samples.append(StatSample(fdn, "utilizationIn", 34.2 if "100G" in port.speed else 41.0, "%", now))
                samples.append(StatSample(fdn, "utilizationOut", 22.8 if "100G" in port.speed else 29.5, "%", now))
    for lsp in lsps.values():
        fdn = f"lsp:{lsp.name}"
        samples.append(StatSample(fdn, "lspOctets", 12_400_000 if lsp.oper == "up" else 0, "bytes", now))
        samples.append(StatSample(fdn, "lspPackets", 98_100 if lsp.oper == "up" else 0, "pkts", now))
        samples.append(StatSample(fdn, "bandwidthReserved", float(lsp.bandwidth_mbps), "Mbps", now))
    return samples

def kv_table(rows: Iterable[tuple[str, Any]], title: str = "") -> Table:

def ls_table(node: Node, path: list[str]) -> RenderableType:
    if not node.children:
        return Text(f"(empty)  {pwd(path)}", style="dim")
    table = Table(
        title=f"{pwd(path)}  [{node.kind}]",
        expand=False,
        border_style="grey37",
    )
    table.add_column("name", style="bold")
    table.add_column("kind", style="cyan")
    table.add_column("label")
    table.add_column("state")
    for name, child in node.children.items():
        st = _object_state(child.payload)
        suffix = "/" if child.children else ""
        table.add_row(name + suffix, child.kind, child.label, state(st) if st else Text(""))
    return table


def tree_view(node: Node, path: list[str], depth: int = 2) -> RenderableType:
    rich = RichTree(f"[bold cyan]{pwd(path)}[/]  [dim]{node.kind}[/]")
    _walk_tree(rich, node, depth)
    return rich


def _walk_tree(rich: RichTree, node: Node, depth: int) -> None:
    if depth <= 0:
        return
    for name, child in node.children.items():
        mark = "/" if child.children else ""
        st = _object_state(child.payload)
        extra = f"  [dim]{child.label}[/]" if child.label else ""
        if st:
            extra += f"  [{SEV_STYLE.get(st, 'white')}]{st}[/]"
        branch = rich.add(f"{name}{mark}{extra}")
        _walk_tree(branch, child, depth - 1)

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import getpass
import os
import secrets
import sys
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from pathlib import Path

from prompt_toolkit import PromptSession
from prompt_toolkit.auto_suggest import AutoSuggestFromHistory
from prompt_toolkit.formatted_text import HTML, StyleAndTextTuples
from prompt_toolkit.history import FileHistory
from prompt_toolkit.styles import Style
from rich.console import Console
from rich.text import Text

from nsp_grok import PRODUCT, RELEASE
from nsp_grok.auth import authenticate
from nsp_grok.commands import Ctx, Outcome, dispatch
from nsp_grok.completer import NspCompleter
from nsp_grok.lab import Store
from nsp_grok.models import User
from nsp_grok.render import SEV_STYLE, banner
from nsp_grok.tree import build_tree, pwd

console = Console()

HISTORY_FILE = Path.home() / ".nsp-grok-history"

PROMPT_STYLE = Style.from_dict(
    {
        "prompt": "ansicyan bold",
        "path": "ansibrightblack",
        "user": "ansigreen",
        "bottom-toolbar": "noreverse bg:#0b1f33 #c8d6e5",
        "bt-key": "bold #6ee7ff",
        "bt-bad": "bold #ff6b6b",
        "bt-ok": "#7dcea0",
    }
)


def _toolbar(ctx: Ctx) -> StyleAndTextTuples:
    visible = ctx.store.visible_nes(ctx.user)
    alarms = [a for a in ctx.store.alarms if not a.cleared and a.ne in visible]
    crit = sum(1 for a in alarms if a.severity == "critical")
    major = sum(1 for a in alarms if a.severity == "major")
    alarm_style = "class:bt-bad" if crit else ("class:bt-key" if major else "class:bt-ok")
    alarm_txt = f"{crit} crit · {major} maj"
    return [
        ("class:bt-key", f" {ctx.user.username} "),
        ("class:bottom-toolbar", "│"),
        ("class:bottom-toolbar", f" {ctx.user.role} "),
        ("class:bottom-toolbar", "│"),
        ("class:bottom-toolbar", f" {pwd(ctx.cwd)} "),
        ("class:bottom-toolbar", "│"),
        (alarm_style, f" {alarm_txt} "),
        ("class:bottom-toolbar", "│"),
        ("class:bottom-toolbar", f" {len(visible)} NEs "),
        ("class:bottom-toolbar", "│"),
        ("class:bt-key", f" NSP {RELEASE} "),
    ]


def _prompt(ctx: Ctx) -> HTML:
    return HTML(
        f"<user>{ctx.user.username}</user> <path>{pwd(ctx.cwd)}</path> <prompt>› </prompt>"
    )


def login_interactive(store: Store) -> User | None:
    console.print(banner())
    console.print(
        Text.from_markup(
            "[dim]Local users: [bold]admin[/]  operator  noc  viewer[/]\n"
            "[dim]Default password:[/] [bold]Nokia123![/]\n"
        )
    )
    for _ in range(5):
        try:
            username = console.input("[cyan]user[/] › ").strip()
            if not username:
                continue
            password = getpass.getpass("password › ")
        except (EOFError, KeyboardInterrupt):
            console.print("\nlogin cancelled")
            return None
        user, err = authenticate(store.users, username, password)
        if user:
            return user
        console.print(Text(err, style="bold red"))
    console.print("[red]too many failed login attempts[/]")
    return None


def login_direct(store: Store, username: str, password: str) -> User | None:
    user, err = authenticate(store.users, username, password)
    if user is None:
        console.print(Text(err, style="bold red"))
    return user


def session_intro(ctx: Ctx) -> None:
    visible = ctx.store.visible_nes(ctx.user)
    alarms = [a for a in ctx.store.alarms if not a.cleared and a.ne in visible]
    crit = sum(1 for a in alarms if a.severity == "critical")
    console.print()
    console.print(
        Text.assemble(
            ("session  ", "dim"),
            (ctx.session_id, "bold cyan"),
            ("  ·  ", "dim"),
            (ctx.user.username, "bold"),
            ("  ·  ", "dim"),
            (ctx.user.role, ""),
            ("  ·  span ", "dim"),
            (", ".join(ctx.user.span) or "ALL", "cyan"),
        )
    )
    console.print(
        Text.assemble(
            (f"{len(visible)} NEs managed", ""),
            ("  ·  ", "dim"),
            (f"{len(ctx.store.lsps)} LSPs", ""),
            ("  ·  ", "dim"),
            (f"{len(ctx.store.services)} services", ""),
            ("  ·  ", "dim"),
            (f"{len(alarms)} alarms", SEV_STYLE["critical"] if crit else ""),
        )
    )
    console.print(
        Text.from_markup(
            "[dim]Type [bold cyan]/help[/] or [bold cyan]ls[/] to start.  "
            "Tab completes.  [bold cyan]/[/] opens commands.[/]\n"
        )
    )


def apply_outcome(out: Outcome) -> bool:
    """Return False if the session should end."""
    if out.error:
        console.print(Text(out.error, style="bold red"))
    if out.clear:
        console.clear()
        console.print(banner())
    if out.renderable is not None:
        console.print(out.renderable)
    return not out.quit


def run_repl(ctx: Ctx) -> None:
    HISTORY_FILE.touch(exist_ok=True)
    session: PromptSession = PromptSession(
        history=FileHistory(str(HISTORY_FILE)),
        auto_suggest=AutoSuggestFromHistory(),
        completer=NspCompleter(ctx),
        complete_while_typing=True,
        style=PROMPT_STYLE,
        bottom_toolbar=lambda: _toolbar(ctx),
    )
    while True:
        try:
            line = session.prompt(_prompt(ctx))
        except KeyboardInterrupt:
            console.print("[dim]^C[/]")
            continue
        except EOFError:
            console.print("\nlogout")
            break
        out = dispatch(ctx, line)
        if not apply_outcome(out):
            console.print("[dim]logout[/]")
            break


def run_batch(ctx: Ctx, commands: list[str]) -> int:
    rc = 0
    for line in commands:
        line = line.strip()
        if not line or line.startswith("#"):
            continue
        console.print(Text(f"{ctx.user.username} {pwd(ctx.cwd)} › {line}", style="dim"))
        out = dispatch(ctx, line)
        apply_outcome(out)
        if out.error:
            rc = 1
        if out.quit:
            break
    return rc


def build_ctx(store: Store, user: User) -> Ctx:
    return Ctx(
        store=store,
        user=user,
        cwd=[],
        root=build_tree(store, user),
        session_id=secrets.token_hex(4),
        started=datetime.now(timezone.utc),
    )


def parse_args(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> argparse.Namespace:
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        prog="nsp-grok",
        description=f"{PRODUCT} {RELEASE} — NFM-P classic management shell",
    )
    p.add_argument("--user", "-u", help="username (skip interactive login)")
    p.add_argument("--password", "-p", help="password (or NSP_GROK_PASSWORD env)")
    p.add_argument(
        "--batch",
        "-c",
        action="append",
        default=[],
        help="run a command non-interactively (repeatable)",
    )
    p.add_argument(
        "--script",
        help="file with one command per line",
    )
    return p.parse_args(argv)


def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
    args = parse_args(argv)
    store = Store()
    password = args.password or os.environ.get("NSP_GROK_PASSWORD", "")
    if args.user:
        user = login_direct(store, args.user, password)
        if user is None:
            return 2
    else:
        user = login_interactive(store)
        if user is None:
            return 2

    ctx = build_ctx(store, user)
    batch: list[str] = list(args.batch)
    if args.script:
        batch.extend(Path(args.script).read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines())

    if batch or not sys.stdin.isatty():
        if not batch and not sys.stdin.isatty():
            batch = sys.stdin.read().splitlines()
        if not args.user:
            console.print(banner())
        session_intro(ctx)
        return run_batch(ctx, batch)

    console.clear()
    console.print(banner())
    session_intro(ctx)
    run_repl(ctx)
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

Shell de gestión **IP/MPLS** inspirado en Nokia **NFM-P / NSP Classic Management 24.11**.

111→3.1 Overview
112→
113→3.1.1 Overview
114→The following communication mechanisms are available to NFM-P OSS clients:
115→• NFM-P XML API and JMS event stream
116→• NSP REST API and Kafka notification service
117→
118→The XML API receives SOAP XML requests for configuring and managing NFM-P system and
119→network objects. The XML JMS event stream allows OSS clients to receive near-real-time
120→notification of NFM-P system and managed-network events. The NSP NFM-P XML API Developer
121→Guide focuses primarily on OSS application integration with the XML API and JMS mechanisms.
122→
123→By subscribing to NSP REST APIs, an NFM-P OSS client can configure and manage objects, and
124→receive near-real-time Kafka event notifications. See theNetwork Developer Portalfor information.
125→
126→Note: The NSP REST APIs also allow OSS clients to integrate with other NSP components.
127→
128→A developer who creates an OSS application for the XML API requires knowledge of the following:
129→• standard XML schema constructions
130→• OSS interfaces
131→• managed devices
132→• NFM-P functions

134→3.2 NFM-P system components
135→
136→3.2.1 Overview
137→An NFM-P system has multiple components. The components are briefly described 1.1 in“NFM-P
138→product overview” (p. 13). For a comprehensive description of NFM-P system components and
139→relationships, see the Component communication information in the NSP Architecture Guide .

177→Clients can monitor events in the NFM-P and the network by subscribing to event streams. This

179→However, the function is unidirectional and does not allow clients to initiate changes in the NFM-P

197→• retrieving network inventory information

227→The JMS events and HTTP requests and responses are written in XML using the SOAP standard.

229→sheets, which are distributed with the documentation. API requests and responses, and JMS events

238→3.4 Secure communication
239→
240→3.4.1 Overview
241→The XML API provides the following functions for secure communication between the OSS clients
242→and the NFM-P:
243→• MD5-hashed passwords for requests
244→• TLS message encryption for JMS events
245→• HTTPS for XML requests and responses
246→
247→Note: MD5-hashed passwords do not secure the communication channel.
248→
249→Note: Nokia recommends enabling TLS for secure communication.
250→
251→TLS is enabled by default on NFM-P server and client interfaces to provide secure communication
252→between NFM-P components. TLS requires a security certificate that is shared among members of
253→a network domain using TLS keystore and truststore files. The NFM-P supports using CA-supplied
254→or self-signed certificates.
255→
256→For backward compatibility, the NFM-P supports non-secure communication with OSS clients. To
257→support non-secure clients, you must disable TLS on the XML API.
258→
259→Note: Disabling TLS on the XML API disables TLS for all clients that use the XML API, and for
260→all NFM-P GUI clients. Browser-based clients are unaffected, and must use HTTPS for
261→application access.
262→
263→See the NSP Installation and Upgrade Guide for information about configuring NFM-P TLS.

275→3.4.2 TLS communication
276→When establishing TLS communication from an OSS system, an NFM-P main server selects the
277→highest security cipher that the OSS client presents. The specific set of supported security ciphers
278→and algorithms may vary, depending on the OSS client and server software components and
279→certificates.
280→
281→You can use an NFM-P tool to specify which TLS versions and ciphers the NFM-P supports. See
282→the procedure to update the supported NFM-P TLS versions and ciphers in NSP the System
283→Administrator Guide for information about using the tool.
284→
285→3.5 TLS message encryption
286→
287→3.5.1 Overview
288→OSS clients can receive secure JMS XML messages using TLS encryption. To enable TLS for an
289→OSS client, you must import a TLS certificate from an NFM-P main server to a TLS truststore file on
290→the OSS client station. You must also configure Java on the OSS client station by specifying the
291→location of the truststore file on the OSS client station. For more information, see the TLS
292→configuration and management information in the NSP Installation and Upgrade Guide .
293→
294→See 4.12 “To compile and connect an NFM-P JMS client” (p.and 62) the Java documentation for
295→information about configuring Java to use TLS.
296→
297→The supported Java version may change between NFM-P releases. A difference in the major or
298→minor Java version can affect operation, for example:
299→• TLS 1.2 is the default security mechanism in Java 8.
300→• In JDK 8u31, the SSLv3 protocol is deactivated.
301→
302→For details about changes to the Java Runtime Environment, see the Java release notes and
303→security documentation.
304→
305→To determine the NFM-P Java version, see4.15 “To determine the Java version” (p. .65)

308→The XML API can send requests and receive responses using HTTPS, which requires TLS
309→encryption. See theNSP Planning Guidefor the system requirements associated with TLS and
310→HTTPS. See theNSP Installation and Upgrade Guide for information about implementing TLS in an
311→NFM-P system.

313→3.5.3 Session management
314→Effective session management requires the AAA functions. Authentication is the verification of a
315→user identification and password. Authorization is the assignment of different levels of access
316→permissions to users. Accounting is the recording of user actions. An NFM-P operator can configure
317→AAA functions using the local security capability of the NFM-P server, a third-party authentication
318→server, or a combination of local and third-party mechanisms.
319→• Local authentication on the NFM-P server is provided by a local user database and security
320→scheme to verify login attempts and assign permission levels for command execution.

344→An NFM-P administrator can use a GUI or OSS client to manage user and group privileges,
345→sessions, and authentication. Using scope of command and span of control profiles, an
346→administrator can specify which functions are available to a user or group, and restrict the objects

348→Administrator Guide for more information.

350→You can configure the following OSS properties of a user account or user group; if the user and
351→group settings differ, the user settings override the group settings:
352→• maximum number of allowed OSS sessions per user
353→• priority assigned to OSS requests
354→• OSS request timeout
355→
356→When the number of concurrent sessions reaches the system maximum, the NFM-P uses the
357→priority values of the outstanding requests to determine which to process next.
358→
359→Note: After an upgrade, the NFM-P assigns the default priority value to each existing OSS
360→user and user group.
361→
362→An OSS request timeout value applies to a request that the NFM-P has accepted but not
363→processed. If the request processing does not begin before the timeout period elapses, the NFM-P
364→rejects the request and returns an error.

237→After you access the XML API Reference, a table appears. The table includes the full package list

247→The information model is a UML drawing that shows the relationships amongst the classes in the

653→ XML schema changes
654→
655→8.8.1 Overview
656→The XML API has evolved over several releases and expanded and changed with the introduction
657→of various network management and network element functions.
658→
659→8.8.2 Deprecated properties and methods
660→Some deprecated objects of the XML API are subject to change or to be replaced, are no longer in
661→use, or were never supported. Although deprecated objects remain in the software, Nokia
662→recommends that OSS developers not use them because the deprecated object may not be
663→included in a future release.
664→
665→8.8.3 Schema changes for releases
666→The differences between releases of the XML API, including additions, deletions, and changes, are
667→listed at a high level. Changes in the schema can be reviewed by examining details of the interface
668→documentation in each release. Differences can be compared to the methods and objects used in
669→OSS applications to determine whether application updates are required.
670→
671→See 8.10 “To view release-specific XML schema changes” (p. 102)for information about viewing
672→schema changes between releases.
673→
674→Note: If you are planning to use an OSS client that was tested in a previous release of the
675→NFM-P, you must review your usage with the list of schema changes before you start
676→development, in order to identify changes that must be made to the packages, classes, types,
677→methods, or properties that are used by the OSS client.
678→
679→8.8.4 Schema changes for network element versions
680→Various packages, classes, and properties may apply to a subset of network element products and
681→versions. Values and applicability of properties may change after a network element upgrade or
682→downgrade. OSS applications should be designed to process XML API such that extra or missing
683→properties do not cause unexpected OSS behavior. For example, OSS applications should not
684→expect specific assigned values for properties that are not applicable to a particular product version.
685→
686→It is recommended that product-specific differences be compared to the methods and objects used
687→in OSS applications to determine whether application updates are required.
688→
689→See 8.5.14 “Supported network elements” (p. 99)for information about products and releases that
690→support a class. Product-specific details may also apply to various properties.
691→
692→Note: If you are planning to use an OSS client that was tested in a previous release of the
693→NFM-P or are planning to use different network element product versions, you must review
694→your usage with the list of schema changes before you start development in order to identify
695→changes that must be made to the packages, classes, types, methods, or properties that are
696→used by the OSS client.

10→5.1.1 Overview

575→ Result filtering
576→
577→6.2.1 Overview
578→Result filters limit the attributes, objects, and child objects that are returned in a result. If no attribute
579→tags are defined in a result filter, then all properties at the level of resultFilter are returned. For more
580→information, see the xmlApiTypes.xsd file in the Schema Reference.
581→
582→The <attribute>propertyName</attribute> tag specifies that the property is to be returned. When
583→using multiple levels of nested resultFilter, a single empty attribute tag <attribute/> returns no
584→attributes for that object level.
585→
586→The <children> list of nested resultFilters</children> tag specifies that the given types of children be
587→returned. The nested resultFilters can contain the class attributes specifying the package qualified
588→class name of the child to be returned.
589→
590→If the children tag is empty, no children are returned. If the children tag is not defined, then all
591→children of this object are returned.
592→
593→The class attribute on nested child resultFilters allows a class of ManageObject to be specified,
594→which is the base class for all classes.
595→
596→If the optional recursive attribute is set to yes in the children specification, then the children are
597→filtered according to the same rules as the parent; nested resultFilters are not required or allowed.
598→The recursive attribute default is no. SeeFigure 6-5, “resultFilter example using recursive children
599→attribute” (p. 78)for an example.
600→
601→Within a nested class resultFilter, by specifying an empty <attribute/> tag, no attributes are returned
602→for the specified class object. However, children and grandchildren of that class object can be
603→returned by including attribute tags with values. SeeFigure 6-7, “Nested resultFilter example
604→specifying only child attributes” (p. 79)for an example.

1045→11.3 Alarm sources

1047→11.3.1 Overview
1048→The sources that initiate NFM-P alarm notifications are:

1051→
1052→11.3.2 Network traps
1053→The NFM-P monitors network health by listening for traps from the managed network elements.
1054→These SNMP traps may indicate conditions that include configuration or operational state changes,
1055→security breach attempts, and equipment faults.
1056→When the NFM-P detects a fault in the network, one or more alarms are generated, depending on
1057→the cause of the fault. When an alarm is created, modified or deleted the JMS messages that
1058→contain the alarm information are sent to interested listeners.
1059→
1060→Note: Although the NFM-P receives network information in traps and generating alarms about
1061→fault conditions in the network, the traps are not directly mapped to alarms.

10→9.1.1 Overview
11→The XML API uses request, response, and fault messages to handle the XML message data related
12→to network objects. Messages are sent to the XML API using an RPC pattern. The messages are
13→constructed and wrapped in a SOAP envelope. The XML API then returns a success response
14→message or a failure fault message.
15→
16→The SOAP encoding transports the XML data. Three types of SOAP messages are used:
17→• requests
18→• responses for a successful or unsuccessful execution
19→• faults for SOAP messages that are not well-formed
20→

10→17.1.1 Overview
11→The XML API can be used to configure the routing and forwarding parameters on NEs. It uses the
12→netw package to configure the contained network elements managed by the network manager.
13→
14→The following network object configurations are required to establish the routing infrastructure and
15→connectivity before services can be provisioned on the network:
16→• network interface
17→• static route
18→• routing protocol
19→• MPLS, LSP and service tunnel
20→
21→17.2 Network interface configuration
22→
23→17.2.1 Overview
24→The network interface represents a virtual router interface in the system. This virtual router interface
25→is defined on a network port. While the physical connection of one device to another is through a
26→port or channel linked by physical wire, it is the network interface that determines the IP
27→connectivity.
28→
29→The XML API uses the rtr package to configure router details. The rtr.NetworkInterface class is
30→created and configured under the parent where the FDN is network:${systemAddress}:router-
31→${*routingInstanceId}:ip-interface-${*id}. It can also include the following parameters:
32→• an IP address and subnet mask associated to a physical port or channel
33→• associated L3 interface to a physical port or channel cabled to another device
34→• configured QoS policy. SeeChapter 18, “Policy configuration management” for more information.
35→• configured routing protocols. See17.5 “Routing protocol configuration” (p. 224)for more
36→information.
37→
38→See the XML API Reference for more information about all of the parameters that can be configured
39→on the classes from rtr package.

90→17.5 Routing protocol configuration
91→
92→17.5.1 Overview
93→A routing protocol specifies how routers communicate with each other, dynamically disseminating
94→information that enables them to select routes between NEs, the choice of the route being done by
95→routing algorithms. The NFM-P supports a variety of standard routing protocols.
96→You can use the XML API to enable and configure network protocol communications and
97→connections on NEs.
98→Supported routing protocols and their packages include:
99→• BGP (bgp)
100→• RIP (rip)
101→• OSPF (ospf)

125→17.5.2 BGP
126→BGP is an inter-AS routing protocol. An AS is a network or a group of devices logically organized
127→and controlled by a common network administration. BGP enables devices to exchange network
128→reachability information. AS paths are the routes to each destination. There are two types of BGP:
129→IBGP and EBGP.
130→• IBGP is used to communicate with peer devices in the same AS.
131→• EBGP is used to communicate with peers in different ASs.
132→
133→17.5.3 RIP
134→RIP is an IGP that uses a distance-vector algorithm to determine the best route to a destination,
135→using hop count as the deciding factor. In order for the protocol to provide complete information
136→about routing, every device in the domain must participate in the protocol. RIP, a UDP-based
137→protocol, updates its neighbors, and the neighbors update their neighbors. RIP directly advertises
138→reachability information to its neighbors by sending prefix, mask, and either hop count or cost metric
139→data.
140→
141→17.5.4 OSPF
142→OSPF is a hierarchical link state protocol. OSPF is an IGP used within large ASs. OSPF routers
143→exchange the state, cost, and other relevant interface information with neighbors after the
144→neighbors are discovered. The information exchange enables all participating routers to establish a
145→network topology map. Each router applies the Dijkstra algorithm to calculate the shortest path to
146→each destination in the network. The resulting OSPF forwarding table is submitted to the routing
147→table manager to calculate the routing table.
148→
149→17.5.5 LDP
150→LDP is used to distribute labels in non-traffic-engineered MPLS applications. Routers can establish
151→LSPs across a network by mapping network-layer routing information directly to the data link layer
152→switched paths. After LDP distributes the labels to the LSR, the LSR assigns the label to a FEC,
153→and then informs all other LSRs in the path about the label and how the label will switch data
154→accordingly.

166→17.5.6 IS-IS
167→IS-IS is a link-state IGP that uses the shortest path first algorithm to determine a route. Routing
168→decisions are made using the link-state information. IS-IS entities include:
169→• networks, which are autonomous system routing domains
170→• intermediate systems (supported routers)
171→• end systems, which are network devices that send and receive PDUs
172→
173→End systems and intermediate system protocols allow NEs to identify each other. The IS-IS protocol
174→sends link-state updates periodically through the network, so each NE can maintain current network
175→topology information.
176→
177→17.5.7 L2TP
178→L2PT is a session-layer protocol that extends the PPP model by allowing L2 and PPP endpoints to
179→reside on different devices that are interconnected by a PSN. L2TP extends the PPP sessions
180→between the CPE and PPP/L2TP termination point (LNS), via an intermediate LAC.
181→
182→17.5.8 RSVP
183→RSVP is a network-control protocol in the IP suite that is used for communicating application QoS
184→requirements to intermediate transit NEs in a network. RSVP uses a soft-state mechanism to
185→maintain path and reservation states on each NE in the reservation path.
186→
187→17.5.9 PIM
188→PIM is a multicast routing architecture that allows the addition of IP multicast routing on existing IP
189→networks. PIM is unicast routing protocol independent and can be operated in the following ways:
190→• sparse mode
191→• dense mode
192→
193→17.5.10 IGMP
194→The XML API uses the igmp package to configure the multicast IGMP routing type on IPv4 hosts
195→and routers. IPv4 hosts and routers use IGMP to report their group memberships to neighboring
196→multicast routers.
197→
198→17.5.11 MSDP
199→MSDP is a protocol that enables multiple PIM-SM domains to communicate with each other using
200→their own RPs. MSDP also enables multiple RPs in a single PIM-SM domain to establish MSDP
201→mesh-groups and to synchronize information between anycast RPs about the active sources being
202→served by each anycast RP peer.
203→
204→17.5.12 MLD
205→MLD is an asymmetric protocol used by IPv6 routers to discover the presence of NEs that wish to
206→receive multicast packets on their directly-attached links, and to discover which multicast addresses
207→are of interest to those neighboring NEs.

403→17.9.3 LSP
404→An LSP is a path through an MPLS network that is set up based on criteria in a forwarding
405→equivalency class, or FEC. LSPs are unidirectional; they enable the label switching of a packet
406→through an MPLS network from one endpoint to another. Bidirectional communication through an
407→MPLS network requires the configuration of an LSP in the opposite direction.
408→
409→17.9.4 Service tunnels
410→A service tunnel is an entity used to uni-directionally direct traffic from one device to another device.
411→The service tunnel is provisioned to use a specific encapsulation method, such as GRE or MPLS,
412→and the services are then mapped to the service tunnel. The most common type of tunnel used in
413→the NFM-P is a service distribution point binding. Service tunnels originate on an SDP on a source
414→NE and terminate at a destination NE.
415→
416→Note: See “MPLS” and “Service tunnels” in the NSP NFM-P Classic Management User Guide
417→for more information about MPLS, LSPs, and service tunnels.

10→15.1.1 Overview
11→OSS applications can use the XML API to perform configuration operations on NFM-P-managed
12→network objects and their associated child objects. This is achieved by sending XML requests that
13→allow the OSS to create, delete, or modify existing objects. These requests can also extend to the
14→object’s children at the same time, if required.
15→
16→Note: The configuration operations that are allowed on each object is defined in the XML
17→schema. See the Schema Reference. See the XML API Reference for more information about
18→the object hierarchies (relationship between parent and child objects).
19→
20→The OSS user account privileges define the access and restrictions for configuration operations in
21→NFM-P functional areas. See the chapter on NFM-P user security in NSP the System Administrator
22→Guide for information about configuring user accounts and assigning privileges.
23→
24→Most of the configuration operations that can be performed on the functional areas of the NFM-P
25→using the GUI can also be performed using the XML API. The main areas for OSS configuration
26→management include:
27→• device configuration—for example, routers, cards, ports, GNE, and channels. ChapterSee 16,
28→“Device configuration management”for more information.
29→• network configuration—for example, protocols, MPLS, service tunnels, and VRRP. ChapterSee
30→17, “Network configuration management” for more information.
31→• policy configuration—for example, service policy, routing policy, and network policy.Chapter See
32→18, “Policy configuration management” for more information.
33→• service configuration—for example, VLL, VPLS, VPRN, VLAN, mirror composite, and customer/
34→subscriber. See Chapter 19, “Service configuration management” for more information.
35→• scripts and template configuration—See Chapter 20, “Script and template configuration
36→management” for more information.

782→15.3.5 Deployment failure recovery procedures
783→The deployment failure recovery procedures to be carried out varies with the type of action
784→(creation, modification, or deletion):
785→• If deployment fails during object creation, you must clear the deployments to remove the
786→previously created object from the database. To remove the possibility of partially-created
787→objects on an NE, resynchronize the object (this can be done using the
788→generic.GenericObject.triggerResync method) and remove all partially-created objects using the
789→XML API or the NFM-P.
790→• If deployment fails during object modification, clearing a deployment does not reset the modified
791→object in the database. To reset to the previous object setting, resynchronize the object. In there
792→are partially-modified objects, set the objects back to their original values using the XML API or
793→the NFM-P.
794→• If deployment fails during object deletion, clearing a deployment completes the object deletion in
795→the NFM-P database. To reset to the previous object setting, resynchronize the object.
796→
797→See 15.4 “Workflow to handle deployment failures” (p. 216)in this chapter for more information
798→about handling a deployment error that has caused the NFM-P database to be out of
799→synchronization with the managed network.

summary.text: I have a comprehensive understanding of the XML API Developer Guide. The user asked me to analyze it as a reference. I'll write a clear Spanish analysis that:

chat_history.content:
Sí, leí el **XML API Developer Guide 24.11** (`3HE-20022-AAAC-TQZZA`). Es la pieza que faltaba: define **cómo un OSS (nuestro shell) habla con el NFM-P**, no cómo se ve la GUI.

## Qué es el XML API

Hay **dos canales**, no uno:

| Canal | Protocolo | Dirección | Para qué |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Request/response** | SOAP XML sobre HTTP(S) `POST /xmlapi/invoke` | bidireccional | inventory, provisionar, ack alarmas |
| **Eventos** | **JMS** (tópicos `5620-SAM-topic-xml-*`) | NFM-P → cliente | alarmas, ObjectCreation, AttributeValueChange, DeployerEvent |

También existe **NSP REST + Kafka**; esta guía se centra en XML/JMS. El cliente puede ser un CLI (exactamente lo que estamos haciendo).

Auth en **cada** SOAP header:

```xml
<security>
  <user>admin</user>
  <password hashed="false">Nokia1234!</password>
</security>
<requestID>nsp-grok@1</requestID>
```

Hace falta rol **OSS Management**. Span of control se aplica en HTTP; en JMS hay que filtrar a mano (`ALA_span like '%:2:%'`).

## Modelo de objetos (lo que importa para el shell)

Todo es `paquete.Clase` + **FDN** (`objectFullName`). El `$core` es la raíz.

| Dominio | Paquetes | Clases típicas |
|---|---|---|
| Equipment | `netw`, `equipment` | `netw.NetworkElement`, `equipment.PhysicalPort`, `equipment.CardSlot` |
| Routing | `rtr`, `ospf`, `isis`, `ldp`, `rsvp`, `bgp` | `rtr.VirtualRouter`, `rtr.NetworkInterface` |
| MPLS | `mpls` | `mpls.Site`, `mpls.Interface`, `mpls.DynamicLSP`, `mpls.ProvisionedPath` |
| Túneles | `svt` | SDP / service tunnel |
| Servicios | `service`, `vprn`, `vpls`, `vll`/`epipe`, `ies`, `subscr` | `svc-mgr:service-ID` |
| Fallos | `fm` | `fm.AlarmObject`, `fm.FaultManager` |
| Stats | `statistics`, `log` | MIB log records |
| Genérico | `generic` | `generic.GenericObject` (CRUD de todo) |

### FDNs reales (Table 10-4)

Hoy el lab usa atajos (`ne:PE-BAIRES-01`). En NFM-P 24.11 son así:

```
network:10.10.1.1
network:10.10.1.1:shelf-1:cardSlot-1:card:daughterCardSlot-1:daughterCard:port-1
network:10.10.1.1:router-1
network:10.10.1.1:router-1:mpls
network:10.10.1.1:router-1:mpls:interface-1
lsp:from-10.10.1.1-id-1
lsp:from-10.10.1.1-id-1:lsppath-2
provisionedMplsTePath:from-10.10.1.1-id-1
svc-mgr:service-100
svc-mgr:service-100:10.10.1.1
subscriber:12
faultManager:network@10.10.1.1@...|alarm-...
```

Nokia recomienda **nunca hardcodear FDNs**: hacer `find` y usar el `objectFullName` que devuelve.

## Métodos que el CLI debería mapear

**Lectura (inventory)**

```xml
<find xmlns="xmlapi_1.0">
  <fullClassName>netw.NetworkElement</fullClassName>
  <filter><equal name="siteId" value="10.10.1.1"/></filter>
  <resultFilter>
    <attribute>objectFullName</attribute>
    <attribute>displayedName</attribute>
    <children recursive="yes"/>
  </resultFilter>
</find>
```

- `find` → `ls` / `show` / `/ne`
- `findToFile` → exports grandes
- `fm.FaultManager.findFaults` → `/alarms`
- `ping` / `version` / `timeStamp` → `/status`

**Escritura (siempre `generic.GenericObject`)**

| Operación | Método | Equivalente en el shell |
|---|---|---|
| modificar | `configureInstanceWithResult` | `show` + edit, `mpls lsp shutdown` |
| crear hijo | `configureChildInstanceWithResult` | `mpls lsp create`, crear Epipe |
| borrar | `deleteInstance` | `mpls lsp delete` |
| CLI al NE | `netw.NetworkElement.executeCli` | sesión CLI (User Guide cap. 10) |

`actionMask`: `create` / `modify` / `delete`. Deploy: `immediate`, sync o async. Si el deploy falla → `generic.DeploymentFailure` + hay que `clearDeployer` y `triggerResync`.

**Alarmas**

- JMS `ObjectCreation` / `AttributeValueChange` con `fm.AlarmInfo`
- Ack/clear: `fm.FaultManager` (`acknowledgeFault`, `clearFaultsOnObject`)

## Workflow MPLS (cap. 17.10) — el que nos importa

Asume IGP ya up en system interface:

1. Enable MPLS en el router + L3 interfaces → `mpls.Site`
2. Asignar network interface a la instancia MPLS → `mpls.Interface`
3. Mesh de **provisioned paths** → `mpls.ProvisionedPath`
4. Mesh de **LSPs** bound a esos paths → `mpls.DynamicLSP` (unidireccional: hay que crear el inverso)
5. **Service tunnels** en ambos sentidos (`svt`) — GRE o MPLS LSP

Después recién vienen VPRN/VPLS/Epipe (cap. 19): customer → service → site → SAP → SDP binding.

## Cómo encaja con NSP-Grok

El shell ya imita esas operaciones; el API dice **el contrato real**:

| Comando actual | Debería terminar siendo |
|---|---|
| `ls` / `cd` / `show` | `find` + `resultFilter` sobre FDN |
| `/ne` | `find` `netw.NetworkElement` |
| `/mpls lsps` | `find` `mpls.DynamicLSP` |
| `mpls lsp create` | `configureChildInstanceWithResult` bajo `network:IP:router-1:mpls` |
| `mpls lsp shutdown` | `configureInstanceWithResult` `administrativeState` |
| `/alarms` + `ack` | `findFaults` + `fm.FaultManager.acknowledgeFault` |
| `/resync` | `generic.GenericObject.triggerResync` |
| `/status` | `ping` + `version` |
| (nuevo) `cli <ne> "..."` | `netw.NetworkElement.executeCli` |

Hoy el lab es in-memory. El siguiente paso natural, con esta guía, es una capa `xmlapi` que arme SOAP, hable con `/xmlapi/invoke`, y deje los mismos comandos.

No toqué código todavía: lo dejaste como referencia. Si querés, el siguiente movimiento es alinear FDNs/clases en el lab y dejar un backend `mock | xmlapi` para cuando tengas un NFM-P real.

Sí, leí el catálogo. No es un Swagger OpenAPI completo: es el inventario que sale de `GET /v1/location/services` de tu NSP vivo. 209 servicios, 1821 endpoints.

El sistema real es **dos backends**, no uno.

| Host | Qué es | Auth |
|---|---|---|
| `https://172.24.80.28:443` | NSP (REST Gateway, Fault Mgmt, Network/Service Supervision) | OAuth2 `POST /v1/auth/token` |
| `https://172.24.80.21:8443/nfm-p/rest/api` | **NFM-P REST** (`samo_*`) | mismo token NSP, o user/pass estilo XML API |

`samo_*` es el XML API de la guía, expuesto como REST. Los nombres de paquete coinciden: `mpls`, `svt`, `fm`, `netw`, `equipment`, `rtr`, `service`.

## Tres capas para el mismo objeto

Para un LSP o un NE hay **tres APIs distintas**. Conviene no mezclarlas:

**1. Lectura rápida (NSP Supervision)** — GET, FDN, árbol

```
GET  /NetworkSupervision/rest/api/v1/networkElements
GET  /NetworkSupervision/rest/api/v1/networkElements/{fdn}/shelves/{shelf}/cards/{card}/ports
GET  /ServiceSupervision/rest/api/v1/nspServices/lsps
GET  /ServiceSupervision/rest/api/v1/nspServices/services
GET  /ServiceSupervision/rest/api/v1/nspServices/tunnels
GET  /FaultManagement/rest/api/v2/alarms
POST /FaultManagement/rest/api/v2/alarms/{alarmFdn}/acknowledgements
```

Esto es lo más parecido a `ls` / `cd` / `show` / `/alarms`.

**2. CRUD genérico NFM-P (el motor)** — cualquier clase, por FDN

```
GET/PUT/DELETE  /nfm-p/rest/api/v1/managedobjects/{fdn}
POST            /nfm-p/rest/api/v1/managedobjects/search
POST            /nfm-p/rest/api/v1/managedobjects/{fdn}/children

POST /nfm-p/rest/api/v2/generic/GenericObject/configureInstanceWithResult
POST /nfm-p/rest/api/v2/generic/GenericObject/configureChildInstanceWithResult
DELETE /nfm-p/rest/api/v2/generic/GenericObject/deleteInstance
POST /nfm-p/rest/api/v2/generic/GenericObject/triggerResync
POST /nfm-p/rest/api/v2/general/find
POST /nfm-p/rest/api/v2/general/ping
GET  /nfm-p/rest/api/v2/general/version
```

Esto es exactamente el cap. 10 y 15 de la guía XML, en REST.

**3. Acciones de dominio NFM-P** — métodos específicos (reboot, turnUp, findRsvpSessions…)

No listan el objeto: **hacen** algo sobre un `instanceFullName` (el FDN).

## Mapeo al shell

| Comando NSP-Grok | API viva que le corresponde |
|---|---|
| login | `POST /rest-gateway/rest/api/v1/auth/token` |
| `/status` | `POST .../general/ping` + `GET .../general/version` |
| `ls` / `find` / `show` | `POST .../general/find` o `POST .../managedobjects/search` |
| `cd equipment/...` | `GET /v1/networkElements/{fdn}/shelves/.../ports` |
| `/ne` | `GET /v1/networkElements` **o** `find` `netw.NetworkElement` |
| `/resync` | `POST .../netw/NetworkElement/fullResync/{fdn}` |
| CLI al NE | `PUT .../netw/NetworkElement/executeCli/{fdn}` |
| `/mpls lsps` | `GET /v1/nspServices/lsps` **o** `find` `mpls.DynamicLsp` |
| `mpls lsp show` | `GET .../managedobjects/{lspFdn}` + `POST .../mpls/Lsp/findServices/{fdn}` |
| `mpls lsp create` | `POST .../generic/GenericObject/configureChildInstanceWithResult` (clase `mpls.DynamicLsp`) |
| `mpls lsp shutdown` | no hay `Lsp/shutDown`; se hace **modify** de `administrativeState` vía generic, o `svt/AbstractTunnel/shutDown` para SDP |
| `/services` | `GET /v1/nspServices/services` |
| `service turnup` | `POST .../service/Service/turnUp/{fdn}` |
| `/alarms` | `GET /FaultManagement/rest/api/v2/alarms` (NSP) **o** `POST .../fm/FaultManager/findFaults` |
| `alarm ack` | `POST /v2/alarms/{fdn}/acknowledgements` **o** `POST .../fm/FaultManager/acknowledgeFault` |
| `/topology` | `samo_topology` (CPAM: SPF, IGP, checkpoints) — no es un mapa ASCII |

## MPLS en tu sistema (`samo_mpls`, 35 endpoints)

Casi todo es **acción sobre instancia**, no listado:

- Config: `Site/configure`, `Interface/configure`, `Tunnel/configure`, `Tunnel/configureTunnelAndPath`, `Crossconnect/configure`
- Relaciones: `Lsp/findServices`, `DynamicLsp/findRsvpSessions`, `DynamicLsp/findCrossconnects`, `Tunnel/findActualPath` / `findProvisionedPath`
- Extra: path optimization, P2MP, SRLG, hops

Listar LSPs **no** está en `samo_mpls`. Se hace con:

- `POST /v2/general/find` + `fullClassName: mpls.DynamicLsp`
- o `GET /v1/nspServices/lsps` (Supervision)

SDP: `samo_svt` sí tiene `AbstractTunnel/turnUp|shutDown`.  
RSVP/LDP: `samo_rsvp`, `samo_ldp` (configure site/interface, find sessions).  
MPLS-TP: `samo_mplstp` (create with autofill).

## Lectura vs escritura (regla práctica)

Para el CLI:

- **Navegar / listar / alarmas / servicios / LSPs** → APIs NSP en `:443` (GET, más simples).
- **Crear / modificar / shutdown / resync / CLI al NE** → NFM-P `samo_*` en `:8443`, sobre todo `managedobjects` + `generic`.

Auth unificado: un token OAuth2 del REST Gateway y se reusa en ambos hosts.

## Qué no está en este JSON

Es un **catálogo de paths**, no los bodies. Faltan schemas de request (`fullClassName`, `filter`, `configInfo`, `actionMask`, FDN). Eso sigue viviendo en la guía XML + XML API Reference.

Cuando quieras, el siguiente paso concreto es un backend `nsp` en el shell: login contra `172.24.80.28`, `ls`/`show` contra Supervision + `find`, y writes contra `generic`/`managedobjects`.
